But do thou lend thine ear, gent le shade of Goldsmith, who didst make thy bear-leader denounce "everything as is ' low ;" and thou, Steele, who didst humanise upon : public-houses and puppet-shows; and Fielding, thou whom the great Richardson. Ivss in that matter, (awl some others) than thyself, did accuse of vulgarity, because thou 411,15 t discern natural gentility in a foot man, and yet was not to be taken , in by the airs of Pamela and my Lady (1. 1. The title is a little startling; but 'style and sentiment." as a lady sail, "can do anything:" Remember, then, gentle render, that talents are not to be dispised in the humblest walks of lire ; we mill add, nor in the muddiest. They tlid not see why they should proceed, but they felt themselves bound to do on; forced conglomerated, crowded onwards, irressistibly Impelled by fate and Jenkins. Often would they have bolted under any other minder. They squeaked and grunted as in ordinary ; they sidled, they shuffled, they half stopped ; they turned an eye to all the little outlets of escape; but in vain.

div.head: WHEIGE WAS I? A STRANGE ADVENTURE. [CONE Lune.]
div.p: WHEIGE WAS I? A STRANGE ADVENTURE. [CONE Lune.]

I sprang sci"h gr,at eagerness up the hill, but my patent hoot were not made d'r sca'ing house-sides, and I had to give it up, and find another way. After a time a defile in the mountain range offered a passage to the , other side, and I speedily followed it out, but only to meet with a repetition of the scenery I had alreadylooked upon—stern dry rugged hills on every band, throwing intensely black shadows. If I stepped into the shade it was frightful darkness, for I could not see any own bands when held before tny eyes. Everything was as silent as the grave; not a hum, not a bird; nor a tree,' flora flower; not even a stream of water—nay, that struck me particularly. Tlave was rota river, a bro dr, or evens puddle of water lobe seen. "Well, this is a 'runt ' shop," I said. "Or rather I'd like it to boa row-shop, for then there would be a chance of getting a drop of liquor of some kind. I'm getting desperately thirsty, not to say hungry. It's all humbug, is this. Yea, testy wish I had Anne humbly, I shall try my palate on these clog-soles soon. There's a rare opening here for some enterprising tradesman. H; need to give a piano away to !tell a pound of tea. Wonder where I am! In Queer-street evidently. Seems to tne I've had the honour of discovering a new world. Humph ! Columbus isn't in it. I could do with his egg. though. I'd be quite willing to bear the yoke then. Wherever can the good folks of this country he? There's not a Manning or a Torn Thumb: scat era dog; a flea or an elephant lobe had for love or money. It appeared to we that the country consisted of nothing but huge mountains arranged in the form of enormous circles, the interior plain, some miles in diameter, being made op of rugged ground with here and flu re a conical hill of the same material. On passing through another rift in the mountain range, I presently found myself standing in the midst of one of there circular plains, entirely Surrounded by. hills as before, but in addition, in the centre of the plant alottytapering peak sprang up. I hastened towards this, hoping to find some signs of habitation or life, but was %gain doomed to disappointment. Complete and profound silence reigned, and everything was motionless "Itch, it's pretty evid at I'm monarch of all I survey, but I'm a jolly sight worse off than Robinson Crusoe. He did block his cabin up with a boat, Ina there's not the least shaving of match-wtad here to build a cabin, let alone a brat. He did leave a parrot to talk to him, but if I shout as loud as a steam blower it will not make the least stir here." A nasty fall which I had at this point stopped my , murmurings, and reminded me that I had better trend more carefully. Looking scrutingisingly around, I found there werea large number of cuttings running in dif- ferent directions across the plains, like so many dried-up .I;in-canals. Wonderif these are some of M.do. Lessep'swork,gieen up far a had Job," I mused. "Wish I could come across , some of the shareholders ; but it's obvious they've all bolted. And yet if anyone had to appear just now I ; should be scared." The ground, as I have already said, was terribly hot, and it may seem strange hew I was able to bear it. Here the absence of air came in useful tome, for, from that cause, the heat received from the blaring globe in the sky did not hang about above the ground, but was rapidly radiated away, no that my limbs were not uncom- forbably warm. I fell to soliloquising again. "How different these iT.ountains Wm to the green
olopea of Old England. 1 Id!tinge Rills and Ribble
Now, if there hnd b?en ;' few

,olinge valleys here, and one or two filtered Mercies, and about bolt .n.dio a parks like ours at home, there would hove been sorne sense In it. N worrier the place is to let, for it seems to have been Iniilt of stone - enishem. Dry, bleak, barren-look- ing scenery! It. all one colour or no colour at all, and the ground as lint ace furnace. Its quite certain you never nerd waren,ua or waterproofs in this country. ! Den in an empty, Med world, for once, nnd how I've got here caps me, cad the thoughts of now tin to get back gives me the creeps. A sixpenny teltgram would boa comfort, but ,ver,hndy's gone on lir, ...

ordido vs, and there's not 'a ghost bf a 'claince of eon ding Word home that I've landed safe." The scenery was getting somewhat monotonous— plenty of towering mountain heights which would haveinade the fortune of Blackpool or Southport ; but they were to grimly stem and bleak that, after the newness had worn off, they became uninteresting. How dift•rent from the Highlands of Scotland !.—that Lender brown heath and sham, wood. Land of thy nonntain and ito 2100 d, or from the richly-varied landscape of the Lake dub

trirt, or even froM the green pastiires and meadows of lAncssliire. I was ins land where there were no waving woods, with the songs of birds of varied plumage; no rolling Ens nr murmuring rivers: no lovely ;lowers or delicious fruits; no gentle bre, 7.P4 or thunderlog hurricanes. As far as the eve could reach I could see nothing but bare rugged mountains, desolate masses of rocks, huge heaps of stones ; nothing to cheer the eye, nothing to relieve . . . . .
the sight, nothing-to rejoice the mind. But tithe surrounding landscape was uninviting in appearance, the magnificent scenery of the heavens above, which I have already hinted at, amply satisfied
lead, or riladdert the

, The clearest night fs England was„ as a fog compared with the pure sky I was stow gazing upon, dotted, mangled, studded, nay, literally crowded, with lustrous diamonds, for every star sparkled with an in- comparable beauty. Venus and Saturn were as magni- ficent discs of light, while the new men shone as an extremely large crescent in the sky, with the old Moon —a massive, dark ball—resting in the con- cavity. And the biasing sphere I have already alluded to appeared as a huge globe of fire noised in space. I could imagine this splendid object tube nothing else than the Sun, though it was difficult to conceive how he could shine so bril- liantly, and, at the naive time, the Moon and stars be visible. Yet I considered this could be ascribed to the same cause as the silence, and the abseece of water, and the absence of heat above tho ground, end the blackness of the shadows, namely, the want of an atmosphere, ter. of course, without air, the nun-tight would not be diffused and refracted in all directions. : and hence the light of the stars would not be out-shone. j It was very handy to set dawn the curious phenomena to this theory, but still it held good for want of a better, and as there was nobody to dispute the point, or debate it with MP, I propleed a resolution, aud car- ried it unanimously that things should be as they seemed to be. In mite of the agility with which I could walk and leap over the land, I presently began to feel fatigued. Ina as I had no wish to be rooted alive I refrained from sitting on the burning ground laid manageto scramble up a little hill, and got an extended view of the country. In one directien the mountains appeared to be more thickly clustend than in another; while on the right a vast pith, stretchH away as far as the eye could reach. hot nowhere was there a sign of habitation, or of any living thine, find with a sigh I ran down to the level stain, a trifle disappointed, a lithe tit anxious for the immediate future, and terribly peekish. I was just beginning to ponder over the interesting problem fif hew I could nonage to subsist on enipty space, which seemed to be the only available commodity ' besides the baked mountain slopes, shen a pecoliar sen- sation in may head began to make ice uneasy. I turned round for relief. Great tigotts! What was coming over we ? I gasped for breath ! It was too true, the air in the apparatus I was menins!, was exhausted ! I could net live! I should perieh ; I should become as one of the lifeless revise! I should never return to tell the

tale! Then I beard the sound of a solemnttoned bell. The first sound I hod heard tin e° coming Into that strange land. Surely it was my death-knell !I A moment more, and all was over, and— I found myself yawning with my head under the easy chair, avid my feet in the enal-senttle ; while the gong of eth clock on the mantel was slowly striking ten ! And. to ! It was n dream ! • • • • • • I hope you will not think this "Stranp Adventure" a swindle. The fact was I had been mailing, before a rusting fire, a chapter nn the moon, and bad dozed over it. Too have cornered me you soy? How ? flow did I manage to see the crescent 'noon in the sky, when on the moat itself, you ask ? Well, it appears that obyict was not the moon at iii; but the globe of the earth re- flecting the sunlight, and appearing like a very large ' ' ' W.ll. K.

In the mienorahle speech which he made in Is4:3,whtn 04.1 prdposed to recognise the Slave-holding ..'onfedeiney of the Sulth, he sent a thrill through to Saise of Commons by a pathetic reference to: his own children and to children born to slavery. Ile said :

W hat aas the state of things before tlo- war? It was this: that every year itt he Slave Stites of Atilt-ries there were one hundred und fifty thousand c'tildrert born into the world- born with the [wigs and tin itom of slavery—born to the liability by law, and by eustom,and by the devilish cupidity of man --to the lash and to the chain awl to the branding iron,and to be taken from their families and carried they know not where. 1 want to know whether you feel as I ft-el Maud this? When lean get down It my home from this House, I find half a dozen lit tle children playing on my hearth. How tunny are there who con say with me, that the most inno- cent, the most pure, the most holy jay which in their past years they huts felt, or in their future years they have hoptcl for, has aris-m Inca contact .n.l association with their own precious children ! If you hot Its., -if, when the heal of Death takes one of those !lowers frotn your home, your heart is overwhelined with sorrow and year household is covered with gloom ; what would it be if your children were brought up to this infernal system ? Think of the one hundred awl fifty thousand little ones every year brought into the Slave States, , among these ti gentlemen," among this tt chivalry,' : among these men who ought to be our friends. We know the cause at this revolt, we know its purpose, and its end. Those who made it have not left the world in darkness respecting their inten- tions. that what the revolt is to accomplish is still hidden from our sight ; anti I will abstain now, as I have always abstained, from predicting what is. to come. I know what I hope for,--what I shall rejoice in,--but I know nothing of future events that will enable met. express a confident opinion. Whether it will give freedom to the race which the white man boo for centuries trampled in the dust, or whether the issue will purify a nation steeped in crime in connexion with its conduct to that race, is known only to the Supreme. In Ilia hands are I alike the breath of men anti the life of States. lam ! willing to commit to Him the issue ot 016 dread contest ; but I implore Him, mid I beseech this House, that my country may lift nor howl nor voice in aid of the most stupendous act of guilt recorded in the annals of mankind.

England was spared the shame of an alliance with the South, and it should never be forgotton that this was in a large measure due to the powerful statement, the convincing argument, aml the noble eloquence of JOHN Blt14:1/T. As an orator, it is not too much to say that, in his palmy days, he was supreme in England—and that is to say in the world. Everything he said was based on the strong common-sense which is the foundation of English character: but he was master lif every feeling and every humour. He could mount in a moment from the common-place to the sabfinie,as when he said—" The angel of death is amongst us; I can almost bear the beating of his wings: He well understood time touch of nature which makes the whole world kin, and he loww how to set the H.onse in a roar with brand hmnour, or apt and witty illustration. But more than the Intel- • loam], it was the moral element in his character which made him strong. He was fearless, indepen- dent, and unselfish. He stood for justice, for free- : dote, rind for truth with unswerving steadiness, and he leaves a name, now that he is gone, which will be cherished and revered as long as our language endures.

Examiner " :and for fourteen years he conducted tlinst journal nsa political and critical organ with great spirit and independence. He was is poet of s no mean order, for ,atly a poet could speak of . • " April with his white hands wet with dowers," or I soy_" Earth for a moment breathes angelic air., His "Atom Ben Adhem " and " The Glove and the Lions " hove already lemons° classical. But it is Os essayist Gait LED. HUNT takes the highest rank. Always cheerful in mood and elegant in expression, the light of his fancy towhes every- thing and brightens everything that it touches. If not as uniformly plaint and humorous as Charles Lamb, he is quaint and hmaorons, and is attractive by showing himself snore ardent as a lover of nature than is the author of the essays of Elsa. What bright things, adorn Isis pages_" like lamps of flowers "—to borrow one of Isis similes. Writing on " Pocket-books and Keepsakes " he says :—" A taste for the very commonest verses, like that for the eommomat tunes on a hand-organ, is an addition to the humanities and serves to keep the best things alive." No one had a keener eye than 1.11,1, HUNT, for what sexy he called the poetry of com- m., things. He looks at a window-pane, and observes In water we behold one of the old primeval mysteries of which the world was made. Thus the cmnsaonest rain-drop on a pane of glass be,nnes a visitor from the solitudes of time." And what snore charaeturistic of the moralist who taught that love of men was love of God than to say—" Kindness itself is the host of all truths." We have spoken of Isis love of flowers, seethe must have loved them, and have wished others to love them who could thus write The fashion of the garments of heaven and earth endures for ever, and you moy adorn your table with speci- mons of their drapery, with flowers out of the fields and golden beans, out of the blue ether." In another column we re-produce the essay " On the Graces and Anxieties of Pig-driving." If there is ',reader who cannot enjoy it, he is, we I fear, intellectually, beyond redemption. There is !, that in LEIIIII HUNT which is not for an ago but for all time. Whilst his stimulates the fancy, lie warms the heart. and leaves men better than Ito finds them.

At the hearing of the case against Mr. W. O'Brien, MR. on Tuesday,Judge Curran startled the agent for Lard Kenumre, and the ielrocate for the Crown, by suggesting a settlement with the tenants. Mr. Healy jumped at the prop. isal to sirbitmte, and suggested two English M.P.s.---one chosen by each party--with Judge Curran as nispire. The in,emt (Mr. Leonard I inidertook to submit the polswal to the trustees, and there the matter stands for the present. It is a new and hopeful sign when a judge in Ireland suggests arbitration it balks like fair-play.

Pigottism seems to hare disorganised the counsel for tha " Times."

IThe traders of Earlestown and Newton are moving, but not very actively, in the matter of opposition to the new railway rates and charges. Fortunately there is now a fair margin of time for going into the subject. The Board of Trade have extended thee for lodging objections to the 3rd of Jane. Meanwhile opposition Viee increased Icharges of the Railway Companies is, week by week, gaining strength throughout the country.

The second reading of the Sunday Closing Bill was carried in the House of Commons, on Wednes- day, by a majorityof 22. This cannot be regarded as other than a great victory for tho temporary:Ai party, seeing that the Home Secretary, whilst remarking that it was not a party question, intimated tbot the Government were not in favour of "Otto uniform rule applicable to the whole country." The Duke of Westminster, who is one of the largest owners of important house property in London, has decided to allow none but certificated plumbers to be employed in future on now build- ings on his estate. This does not moan that there will be no more had work out of sight ; but the certificate is, or ought to boo. assurance that bad work will not at any rate, be a consequence of sheer incompetence,

THE treatment of Irish political prisoners has led to comparison with the way in which LEIGH HUNT and his brother JOHN wore treated during their incarceration for two years, for a political libel, ptiblished in 1812, in the columns of the London "Examiner". The libel was contained in an article written by Laical first which, commenting on 11, fulsome panegyric on the PRINCE REGENT, asked who would suppose that " this Adonis in Loveliness was a corpulent gentleman of fifty." JOHN HCNT Was proprietor of the "Examiner," and he was therefore committal to gaol for two years along with his brother. It has always been under- stood that Lanai HUNT had an easy timeof it while in prison; and his case has therefore been cited by way of contrast to the barbarities which have been inflicted on Mr. WILLI %II O'BRIEN and other Irishmen now suffering for conscience' sake. But , a writer in the "Daily News " expressed himself, the other day, as sceptical as to the statement that the brilliant essayist was treated with kindness whilst in Horsemonger Gaol. There was mismanagement in the Navy in the days of Charles the Second. Macaulay says Pepys, who made a report on the mbject, " informed his master that the Naval Administration was a prodigy of wastefulness, corruption, ignorance, and indolence, that no estimate could be trusted, that no contract was performed, that no check was enforced." This report was made in In,t4. Alter the date to 1889, mid the report may stood; there is nothing new under the sun—in the mismanage- ment of the Navy. It is satisfactory to me from the discussion, on Tuesday in the Rouse of Commons, on the Civil Service estimates, that the Radical iambus ere , alive to resisting ocpendittire on palaces, as Mr. I Labouchere put It," not in the oompation of her Majesty." A protest was made, too, against the I exclusion of the public from the greater portion of Hampton Court Park, and Mr. Minket pro- mised to see what could be done in the matter. There is nothing like "pegging away " at these grievances,

" Shorter Parliaments "—that is the cry when it is seen that a Government may cling to office for years after they have forfeited the confidence of the conntry. Election campaigns ought also to lbe shortened. At the meeting in London, on Wednesday, of the Association of Chambers of Commerce a resolotholl Was pittiSe d declaring that lit was desirable, in view of the hindrance !occasioned to trade, that the period over which general Parliamentary elections extend should be considerably shortened.

'Co help tu draw, a Church Army has been introaluiml, persons ilesirims of enrolling are to attend elturelt on Sunday next, when the bells will ring to welmone tin-at I providisl the ringers are paid, and on All F•sals* day following they mav enjoy a ham tea h the small sum of sixpence. The liospel feast not being , sufficiently well laid liefore the masses, there is to to carnal fis;st, and. strangest of all, pig's flesh during Lent by clergy who adopt 8 a.m. low 111.9 or fasting com- munion. Let us hope that they are beginning to get a little light by seeing that meats pnwit nothing, but rather that they are created to be received with thanks- giving by the faithful, and by them that have known the truth. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN.

B;AN 6t'CA-SIONAL COURESPONDENT. That it is hoped the overseers will not allow the question of the Ship Canal assessment,raised at the vestry meeting,to quietly drop out of consideration. From the remarks of Mr. I mison it is quite clear that the ratepayers of Runcorn have suffered an injustice. In round figures the assessment was increased from 1:6.000 to £1,300, and basing their rate upon tins increase, the Guardians made a heavier call upon the Ittincorn overseers than other- wise would have been the case. That the Ship Canal Company were successful in their appeal against the increase in the assessment, which was practically reduced below the original figure, and the ovemeers to meet the heavier call, had to fall hack upon the ordinary ratepayers. That in fact Runcorn has contributed tothe Union expenses about £llOO more than was just or right, and the other townships in the Union have benefited to that extent. That the point contended for is this When the next call is made Runcorn must be credited with the amount orerpaid, and the representatives of the town on the Board ought to use their influence to attain that end. That the "nice little bill" presented by the Slop Canal Companv for their expenses in the appeal is over .Cl,BOO. This SUM added to an equal amount (perhaps more) for the costs of the Board of Guar- dians in the matter will make an addition to the rates that will press severely these hard times. That the Ship Canal is evidently not an unmixed blessing. That at the meeting of the Board of Commis- sioners on Thursday next the public ought to be placed in possession of the facts with regard to Waterloo Bridge, and the proposed improvements. At the last meeting there was an evident desire and intention to condlict the wl,olu affair in camera, and in these enlightened days the people's eepreeeu- irr all matters ought to be above board. The amount of shelving that has tak,n place over this matter is not creditable to any body of business

men. That now the " ethereal mildness" of spring is coming, one is inclined to ask " Where are the Runcorn Baths?" The answer is easy "Far, far away." That the courteous and painstaking Secretary to the Board of Commissioners i 4 to be granted an! increase of salary at the next meeting--.£17,1 to I'2oo, and no one can say that he is not deserving of it, for the responsible position he occupied. That an incident which mild be taken ewe gram maig, occurred on Runcorn Bridge on Saturday night last. About midnight a young man was on the bridge on his way home from Widnes, when a man having the appearanc,. of a navvy struck him a blow on the chest and demanded ho. Somewhat startled the young !eau had, however, presence of mind to parley with his assailant, who brought him up short by saying if he aid not produce the required sera, he would be thrown over the bridge into the river below. Stepping back, the young man pretended to draw the trigger of a revolver. I and presenting his gloved finger at the " cowardly miscreant's " head, Hi, wetted to blow out hi, , brains if Is. ,list not allow him to pass. The would. be robber fell back in amazement and the young ! man walked away with his one, in, act. That of course the night was dark and the navvy might have been near sighted , but apart from the : gloved finger incident, there is no doubt that the Bridge is a very dangerous thoroughfare after dark.l Those who have occa-ion to use the Bridge at a ! late hour, know the rough characters that are to be met with, and they have been much more num- erous during the past twelvemonths. The Railway ' Company charge a very heavy --in fact an extor- tionate price for walking to and from Widnes, and they ought to provide protection for their passengers. A watchman ought to patrol the Bridge nightly, so as to be within call in case of any out- rage ; and there is not the slightest doubt that the profits made would amply afford the payment of his wes. Thatag there have been outrages on the structure and probably will he again, and it is a perfect " Bridge ef Terrors" to th, timid and nervous. That the Widnes Local Board election will be decided on Saturday next, when it is confidently expected that the retiring members, with the addition of young Mr. Timmis will be the success- ful candidates. That the Liberal meeting on Monday evening was one of the most successful held in the town for some time past; and the enthusiasm of the crowded audience was a treat to Witness.

Linaker, on the 27th instant: —Acton Orange, Mr. Tliomws Hewitt; Alvanley, Mr. Henry Lowe ; Antrohus, Rev John Newell Tanner ; Appleton, Messrs. William Hewitt and Joseph Knowles; Aston, Mr. William Wilkinson ; Bartington, Mr. Enoch Jackson; Budworth. Mr. John Mclntyre; Clifton, Mr. Joseph Stoles ; Crowley, Mr. James Whitlow; Daresbury, and Keckwick, Mr. Thomas Warburton ; Dutton, Mr. John Campkin Frodsharn, Messrs. John Ashton, and Henry Edward Heywood; Frodsham Lordship, Mr. Thomas Limit ; Halton, Mr. John Baguley Hatton, Mr. Jame. Parr; Helsby, Mr. James Israndreth ; Kingsley, Mr. Peter Hall ; Kingswood, Mr. John Harrison ; Manley, Mr. Mark Mounfield ; Moore, Mr. Thomas Forster; Newtons by-Daresbury, Mr. Eaton Bretherton ; Newton-by-Prod- sham, Mr. Joseph Hall ; Morley. Rev. C. R. Nunn and Mr. William Pickering ; Norton and Stoeldiam. Mr. Jos. W. Baguley Prestomo,th%lfill, Mr. William Whitlow ; Runcorn, Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. H. J. Grier, H. D. Jones, Samuel Taylor, Philip Speakman, Joseph Jeffs. John J. Waterworth, George Bellamy, Peter Smith, and Joseph Pritchard ; Seven Oaks, Mr. William Clarke; Stretton, Mr. Joseph Smith; Sutton, Mr. Edmund A. Wallington ; Walton Inferior, Mr. John Weir; Walton Superior, Mr. W. Turner; Weston, Messre, Edward Aaron and John W. Kirkham; Whitley Inferior, Mr. Charles Mounfield . • and Whitley Superior, Mr. George Priestner. It will be otwerved that there are ten gentbsnen nomi- nated for the five seats to which Runcorn is entitled. The returning officer has ruled that Dr. Gastaldi and Mr. Pritchard are not eligible as Guardians because they do not occupy premises rated at £255 year. As smatter of fact it is stated that both gentlemen are rated ss. below that figure. Unless there are three withdrawals a contmt must take place. The retiring Guardians are! nominated with the exception of Mr. J. W. Lightbursu : who through an oversight will be debarred from appeal- ing for the sußmges of the ratepayers. His genial presence will he much missed by the inmates of the Workhouse on Board days.

div.head: RT. HON. JOHN BRIGHT, M.P. (From Photograph by the London Stereoscopic Company).
div.p: RT. HON. JOHN BRIGHT, M.P. (From Photograph by the London Stereoscopic Company).

DEATH. OF MR. BRIGHT. THE CLOSING SCENE. On Wednesday morning, at 25 minutes past eight, , Mr. John Bright, after being in a semi-unconscioun! state for sixteen hours, peacefully expired. The , cause of death was Bright's disease, complicated by diabetes. There was no return of consciousness before death. The aged statesman calmly, without ' pain ansi almost imperceptibly, ceased to breathe. All his family were at his bedside at thelast, except- ing Mrs. Cash, who arrived shortly. afterwards. keom half-past five on Tuesday evening he took nothing but water, and the only words which escaped his lips from that time were expressions of thanks to those who administered it. He was con- scious of his approaching death, for lie referred to the event on Sunday, stating that he was convinced !he should not recover. Knowledge of the fact did not in any way appear to disturb his mind ; indeed, when he was apprised of the coming change it had no sorrowful effect upon him, but he became cheer- fully resigned. We give iii another part of the paper a sketch of Mr. Bright's career. A correspondent telegraphing on Tuesday evening said : At dawn of day it was noticed that a change for the worse had occurred in the condition of the patient. Tne decay of his line constitution has been ! gradual but continuous. Ile has never been quitel convalescent since the attack on the 28th of slay,, 1888. The illness from which he then suffered temporarily gave way to medical treatment, and he I rallied somewhat during the summer months, recovering so much that in July he was able to I enjoy the bracing air of his garden. As September advanced he seemed to improve. The Hush of health upon his cheeks was destined to fade, lot when chill! October set in his progress was abruptly checked. , During the prevalence of east winds lie contracted a severe chill. Pulmonary symptoms succeeded, and from that time forward he has suffered with varying intensity. Though he has been able at times to sit in li is ante-chamber, and to remain in his lounging-chair j for two or three hours a day, he has never rallied entficiently to leave Iris room. Throughout his pro- , traeted illness his pet dog has been his constant companion. During the last few weeks he has sometimes beets well enough to read a newspaper, and he retainest much as Iris powerful voice until Sunday last. Its spoke easily, though faintly, up to A onday. The symptoms then became alarming. and were accompanied once or twice by vertigo. Happily during the greater part of the time he was lieu from pain, but suffered from the lassitude inevitable in eases where the patient is too weak to sit up. The history of his iitrreoa is a record of! manly fortitude and resignation. Ile has exhibited , rare patience and kindliness to all who have waited upon him. As the hours passed on Tuesday morn- ing the change became more serious, sat il his con- dition was pronounced by Dr. Ilayle, who had been in attendance from the previous evening, to be one of great prostration. The spark of life was, Ire said, fast waning. Mr. Bright from six n'elock on Monday evening has not been able to take nourishment. his consciousness remained, and to members of Iris family who visited his bedside in the morning he bade farewell. The weather on Tues- day was pleasant and seasoliable, the sun gilding the bedroom of the statesman, the walks of whose garden were fretted with blooming crocuses, and the lawn sleeked with emerald green of the , young springing grass, while from the fulness One Ash Tree, within the bearing of the hushed chamber, a robin sang it plaintive lay. About three ! in the afternoon, Mr. Bright began to sleep fitfully. When awake he wns occasionally unconcious. Mr. Leathern Bright arrived about Tue,day noon ! from Scotland, having just returned from Russia. At his interview with his father, Ise said that the proprietor of the hotel WhOrt, Mr. Bright nevi to stay on his fishing excursions in Scotland had sent a message of the det pest sympathy with him in his illness. Mr. Bright was then perfectly conscious. and recognised the gentleman referred to as Sandie M'Cann. Mr. Phillip Bright, the youngest non, arrived about four in the afternoon from London. His father, who waa still conscious at intervals, recognised him, and was evidently pleased to see him. Mr. Thomas Bright, who iv himself suffering ' trom a severe cold, went to we his brother, and was almost prostrated to see the change that hail taken place. SO great indeed was the change that , persons who had not seen Mt. Bright during his ill- ness would almost fail to recognise lain. Ilia fea- tures had shrunk and become greatly altered. About half-past six on Tuesday evening Mrs. Currie, ! one of Mr. Bright'a daughters, arrived. Mrs. Clark I and Mrs. Roth, his other two slaughters, and Mr. John Albert Bright were present. Whenever Ise showed distinct consciousness fie almost invariably !asked for a drink of water, and, on being supplied with this, he thanked the person who bad waited upon him, and relapsed into unconsciousnese. lie appeared to have a craving for draughts of cold water during the last hours of his life, and told the doctor that he enjoyed it better than anything else. [During the seven or eight hours which immediately preceded death Mr. Bright dirt not speak, and the indications sif approaching dissolution became rapidly more marked He finally passed away as though in sleep. At eight o'clock on Tuesday evening, a telegraph message of deep sympathy and inquiry was received from the Prince and Princess of Wales; but at that time he was unconscious, unit had been so for hours. Mr. J. A. Bright immediately answered the message. A telegram of inquiry was also received from the Queen.

MESSAGES OF SYMPATHY. Many sympathetic messages, int...lmbue' one (min Her Majesty, were received at One Ash on Thursday, and from all parts of the country came expressions fit' grief d sorrow at Mr. John Bright's death. On Thursday , night the workpeople l height Brothers met in the mill , yard at Rochdale and adoptel an address of condolence, and also resolved that a memorial tablet should be placed lin the Free Library, or other local building. It was 1 further suggested that a statue 01 51.0 statesmanwho had lived such a noble life anumg the Lancashire people should be erected in the town. FUNERAL ARRANGEMEN'TS.

..... It inn singular coincidence that Weshiesday seas the sixteenth anniversary of 'the death of Mr. Samuel Bright, brother of Mr. John Bright. The graveyard attached to the Friends Meetinghouse in Roolidale is the burying- r ' place of the Bright family, and hero the deceased Matt,- I man has chosen to be intornsl. The sanctuary ion most unpretentious little stonebuilding, and in the graveyard attached rest the remains of hit father. Ws mother, his wife, sisters, and leathers. The funeral is fined for eleven on Saturday morning. From its very limited site the Meeting floss. is unable to accommodate more than the inunediate family and friends. Because of this, and also becauie of the expresses' with of Mr. Bright himself, it it the desire of the family that the funeral shall be in every way as quiet and private as , possible, and without wreaths or 'lowers. Admission will baby ticket. The Mayor of Rochdale, Mr. Jolla Edward Petrie, has invited the members of the Town Council to meet him at the Town Halton Saturdaymorn. , inn and join tin funeral cortege in One Ash. Step.

being taken Iry.llr.r public bodies to secum representa- tion at the ceremony, the Rochdale Reform Association, which held a meeting on Wednesday night, being o.e of the fimt tomove in the matter. A deputation from the : workpeopleof Messrs. Bright Brothers waited upon Mr. J. Albert Bright with a request that thee might be per- mitted to join the funeral cortege, :Ina there is every likelihood of the suggestion being carried out. Mrs. Gladstone and Mr. Alundella,amongst others, on Wednes- day sent telegrams of condolence. A successful caste id Mr. Bright's head has, at the reipmqt of the family, been taken by Mr. Bruce Joy.

RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY The fortnightly meeting of this authority- woe held at Dutton Workhouse on Thursday, when there were present —Colonel Ashton (chairman), Messrs. E. Aaron, J. Stokes, J. Baguloy, T. Lewis, W. Hewitt, C. Mounfield, l'. Hall, Brandrnth, J. Hall, W. Pickering, li. Linaker (clerk), 11. G. Linaker (assistant clerk), and J. Farrington (sanitary inspector). 'recoil stoo Ilsonxce.—The Clerk reported that there was a balance of £1.,130 Os. sd. in the hands of the treasurer in favour of the Board. Tan Oterstosnz or Ism-nous Disease.—Dr. Adams, the medical officer of health, presented a special report to the authority stating that in reference to the outbreak of scarlet fever at Stockton Heath, which had been the subject of a previous report, he had to report that about 26 fresh cases had cane under his cognizance, thus making about 43 eases in all. The schools had been closed for one month, and permission to re-open then: had been gran' ed, as most of the eases were convalescent. The usual measures had beer: taken to prevent extension of the disease. Ile had also to report that at Weston Points ease of typhoid fever had occurred, the patient being a nian who had been working outside the district with his brother, who had also con- tracted the disease. The infection must, therefore, be regards' as imported. The usual preventive meaenres had been adopted in this case. Ile had also to reliort that an alleged outbreak of infectious disease had occurred in the township of Acton Grange. He had visited the premises, and had inspected the patients, but had failed to discover any speeitic traces of infectious diseases, but as the disease had been attributed by the private medical attendant to the water supply, and as , the' possible pollution of the:water supply to the premises had been the subject of previous special reports (and on which legal action had been taken with results which up , • to the present hail keen comparatively futile), he would , suggest that Hie water supply to the premises be , analysed, and that a reporton that water be presented to , the authority in order that further action might b.; taken if necessary for the provision of an improved water , supply. Ocerratio Rousso AT Wes-Inv.—The Inspector reported ' that certain houses eituate in this township were with- outs water supply, and orders were given for notice to be served for a supply tithe provided. :NUISANCE AT WALTON larnamia—A nuisance was reported as existing in this township arising from defective drainage. The Inspector stated that he had seen the owner respecting the matter, and he had received a promise that it should be attenchnl to. FARM raluisso AT ACTON tillANGE.—The Inspector was directed to obtain a sample of the water at certain form premise, situate in this township and submit the seine Ness anlaysis. 1101,F.S.—CertitiCAte: of occupation for new houses were granted to Mr. John Howard, of Rimeorn, for a new Iv Rise elected by hint at Frodsham ; also to Mr. William Twiss, of Warrington, for fair hoses erected by l ill, at Wilderspool ; also to Mr. Janos Warbur•on, of Stockton Heath, for five houses erected ftc hint at the some place ; and also to the direetors of the Solt Union, for a house erected by them at Weston This was the whole of the business.

RAILWAY ROBBERIES AT WIDNES. At Whines Petty Suasion on Thursday, before Mr. F. 11. Gossage and Mr. 11 Wade-Deacon, Jas. Swims and Mary Ann Stokes, man and wife of Old Marsh, , were charged with having stolen on the 24th Jan., 34 yards of floor carpet, 414 yards of stair carpet. 64 yards of oil cloth, one gross of tape and one , canvas wrapper, value XI 10s. 4td. the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company. : Edward Walker and his wife Annie of 2la back Parliament-st., Liverpool. were Rhoo charged with stealing the goods. and with receiving them know- ing them to have been stolen. Mr. Preston Jun., prosecuted, and stated that the Company had for some time suffered great loss through robberies of this description. lie called Frederick Tebbutt, draper. Anne-et., West. In a crowded House Mr.-171+.'S;;;:ra use urn! with much I feeling, referred to the death of Mr. John Bright. Ile said the event was one of profound sorrow to every member ef the House and every subject of the Queen. He referred to his great pirxer in debate, his generosity to his opponents, and with evident emotion said Mr. Bright would go to IHS grave honoured by the affection it friends anil opponents, and that he would leave behind him a name which would be graven in history long after this Parliament had passed away. Mr. GLADSTONE followed, and in eloquent terms, he referred to the deceased statesman's splendid eloquence, which, ho said, was as lofty as Lid ever sounded in those wano. He feelingly alluded to the difference of opinien that existed between himself and Mr. Bright, and, in glowing terms, referred to the brilliant quahties of Mr. Bright as a Matmman, the grand simplicity of his character, and his sterling qualities as a tnan that made hint ha wed by all classes of his countrymen. Lord HARTINOTON said Mr. Bright went to his grave amid .the veneration of his fellow countrymen.—Mr. JUSTIN MCCAIITHT and Mr. CHAMBERLAIN paid tribute to Mr. Bright as one of England's greatmt statesmen. THE MANCHESTER. SHIP CANAL. WESTON.

River work is still at a standstill on this section, but satisfactory progress k being made with the cutting on Frodsham Marsh, and with the construction of the great , lock at the mouth of thir Weaver. There is nothing new TO report. RUNCORN. Operations love been very quiet in this section this week. At No Man's Land there has been a total cessation of work, but a little higher up the river the pile driver has been actively engaged on two or three days. The task of clearing away the rock on the Widnes shore ha. also been suspended. Good progrms is being made at Norton with Randell's sluice.

FRESH OPPOSITION FROM LIVERPOOL. A London cornspondent says hear from a legal source that a fresh attack is about to be opened by the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board upon the Manchester Ship Canal. On Friday, it is mid, an application will be made to Mr. Justice Chitty for an injunction against the Canal Company to stop the work in pmgrees between Eastham and Runcorn, the allegation being that in several partienlars the company have deviated from the scheme laid down in the Act under whichtlair operations , are being condocted. It is, of course, impossible to anticipate the result of the action ; but your readers will doubtless be inclined to believe that the men who have hitherto steered the great undertaking with such magnifittent success, in spite of the attacks made upon it, have not serioUsly compromised their position. The pity of it is that more money should be wasted in what, from all lean gather, seems lobe an attempt to obstruct the program; of the canal.
